turns.t: Hi! Right, lupus review. I think I'm doing okay, but you tell me. I've also got a rash on my cheeks that's come back.
Good to see you. Let's start with the rash. When did it come back?
About two weeks ago. Across my cheeks and nose, a butterfly thing. It's worse in the sun.
Any joint pains? ~
A bit, in my hands, in the mornings. Nothing too bad. ~
Let's check what you're taking.
Hydroxychloroquine, 200 mg twice a day. Prednisolone, 5 mg, once a day. And a calcium and vitamin D tablet, once a day, for my bones.
Good, that matches. Any fever, or mouth ulcers, or chest pain when you breathe in?
No, none.
And what do you do for work, are you outdoors?
I'm a postwoman, so yes, outdoors most days.
That could well be the sun triggering the rash. Let me look. ~
Go on.
There's a pink, slightly raised rash across both cheeks and the bridge of your nose, and the skin elsewhere on the face is clear.
Is it a flare? ~
With the sun-sensitive rash and a bit of morning hand stiffness, I'd say this is a mild flare of your lupus.
Do I need more tablets? ~
Not today. Your current treatment is covering you, and I'd rather get the sun protection right first. ~
I wear a hat. ~
A hat's good, but you need a high-factor sun cream, factor 50, on your face, every day, even when it's cloudy.
Every day? Even in winter? ~
Yes, because UV gets through cloud. And long sleeves on your arms when you're on your round. ~
Right. And what about my eyes, the hydroxychloroquine? ~
You should have your yearly eye check, so I'll make sure that's booked.
Good, I was going to ask. ~
If the rash spreads, you get a fever, mouth ulcers, swollen ankles, or your urine goes frothy or dark, ring me and come in.
Right. I'll watch for those. ~
Keep taking everything as you are. ~
Thanks, doctor, it's always good to talk it through. ~
Take care, and mind the sun. ~
